lab_title: Shaping Molecules: Predicting Molecular Geometry with VSEPR Theory
top_level_objectives: Explain the central principle of VSEPR theory: that electron domains around a central atom arrange to minimize mutual repulsion
Translate a Lewis structure into an electron-domain count and identify the corresponding electron-domain geometry
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry and predict how lone pairs alter observed molecular shape
Identify the five fundamental electron-domain geometries and the common molecular shapes derived from them
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs and account for bond-angle deviations from idealized values
Compare VSEPR predictions to the observed structures of real molecules such as water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, and XeF4

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the fundamental premise of VSEPR theory that electron domains repel one another and settle into arrangements that maximize their separation in space.
key_visuals: A single central atom sphere at the center of the workspace with a few glowing electron-pair clouds hovering around it
Animated repulsion vectors pushing the electron clouds apart until they reach a stable spread
A simple on-screen definition panel stating the VSEPR principle
student_actions: Grab and drag electron-pair clouds toward one another and release them to watch them spring back to a minimum-repulsion arrangement
Read the introductory principle and tap to confirm understanding before advancing

scenes.scene_name: From Lewis Structure to Electron Domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Bridge prior knowledge by showing students how to count electron domains (bonding groups plus lone pairs) directly from a Lewis structure.
key_visuals: A flat 2D Lewis structure of a sample molecule floating beside its emerging 3D central atom
Highlighted bonding pairs and lone pairs color-coded to distinguish the two types of domains
A running domain-count tally displayed as a label
student_actions: Tap each bond and lone pair in the Lewis structure to tag it as an electron domain
Sort the tagged domains into bonding versus lone-pair categories to complete the domain count

scenes.brief_purpose: Establish the five fundamental electron-domain geometries that arise as the number of domains increases from two to six.
key_visuals: A central atom that gains one bonding domain at a time, morphing through linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral arrangements
Ideal bond angles labeled at each stage (180 degrees, 120 degrees, 109.5 degrees, and the 90/120 degree mix)
A carousel of the five geometry names with their domain counts
student_actions: Add and remove bonding domains around the central atom and observe the geometry reorganize to minimize repulsion
Match each resulting arrangement to its correct geometry name and ideal bond angle

scenes.brief_purpose: Teach the distinction between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry by converting bonding domains into lone pairs and observing the resulting common shapes.
key_visuals: A tetrahedral central atom whose bonding domains are swapped one by one into lone pairs, revealing trigonal pyramidal then bent shapes
Side-by-side derivation of seesaw, T-shaped, and linear from trigonal bipyramidal, and square pyramidal and square planar from octahedral
Ghosted lone-pair clouds shown as larger, more diffuse than bonding domains
student_actions: Toggle individual bonding domains into lone pairs and watch the molecular shape update
Name the molecular geometry that results after each lone-pair substitution

scenes.brief_purpose: Explain that lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, producing measurable deviations from idealized bond angles.
key_visuals: A comparison of methane and water central atoms with live bond-angle readouts showing 109.5 degrees versus 104.5 degrees
An exaggerated, enlarged lone-pair cloud visibly compressing the adjacent bonding angles
An angle-slider showing how bond angle shrinks as lone-pair count rises
student_actions: Compare the measured bond angles of methane, ammonia, and water side by side
Predict whether adding a lone pair will increase or decrease the bond angle, then reveal the actual value

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate learning by having students apply VSEPR to real molecules and compare their predictions to observed experimental structures.
key_visuals: A gallery of real molecules water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, and XeF4 rendered as 3D ball-and-stick models
A prediction panel where the student selects electron-domain geometry and molecular shape before the true structure is overlaid
Green or red confirmation markers indicating whether each prediction matched the observed geometry
student_actions: Work through each molecule by predicting its electron-domain geometry and molecular shape from its formula
Overlay the observed 3D structure to confirm the prediction and review any mismatches
